author: Claude (English teacher role), drafted directly (Gemini quota exhausted for this session)
basis: New mission, no workbook source; written per docs/plans/new-mission-playbook.md, angle distinct from sdg1 (general safety-net framing) and sdg1-2 (labor-market framing): social mobility and scholarships specifically. Facts and sources: NTU economics department study using national tax records for the 1993-1995 birth cohort found a child from a rich household is about six times more likely to be admitted to NTU than a child from a poor household; NTU/public-university students' median household income (NTU >NT$1.5M, other public universities >NT$1M) far above the overall sample median (~NT$860,000), producing a 'reverse redistribution' effect since elite public universities receive more government funding per student (報導者/The Reporter coverage of the NTU study, also covered by 商業周刊/今周刊). Stars Program (繁星計畫): multi-track admission by in-school standing rather than only national exam score, designed to widen access for rural/under-resourced students. Ministry of Education's University System Financial Aid Program for Disadvantaged Students (大專校院不利處境學生助學計畫), since the 2007 academic year, targets households in the bottom 40% of income distribution with four kinds of support: tuition subsidy, living stipend, emergency relief, housing subsidy (教育部圓夢助學網/coloan.moe.gov.tw). Early-intervention argument sourced to 獨立評論 commentary on rural education and poverty. Cram-school spending advantage and post-admission cost burden stated in general terms, not invented as precise figures.

slides.1: Here's a fact that should surprise nobody, yet still does. A rich student is about six times more likely to get into Taiwan's top university than a poor student is.
slides.2: SDG 1 aims to end poverty everywhere, and this talk focuses on the one tool people always praise: education. Does school actually break the cycle that passes poverty to the next generation?
slides.3: Look closely at the numbers behind admission. Students at Taiwan's top university usually come from homes earning more than NT$1.5 million a year, far above most Taiwan families.
slides.4: Wealthier families pay for private lessons after school, and that practice shapes how well a child does on the exams that decide entry. Poorer families often cannot afford the same head start.
slides.5: Here is a strange twist: Taiwan's top public universities receive more government funding per student. Yet their student body tends to come from richer homes than average. The system meant to balance things does the opposite.
slides.6: Even after admission, a low-income student still faces real costs: tuition, textbooks, and rent all add up fast. Time spent studying is also time they cannot spend earning money.
slides.7: Here is some genuine progress. Taiwan has built the Stars Program, which judges a student by their ranking inside their own secondary school rather than by one national exam alone.
slides.8: Taiwan has also run a wider aid plan since 2007. It offers tuition help, living costs, and even housing support to students from the poorest forty percent of households.
slides.9: Money alone rarely solves the whole problem. A scholarship works far better when it arrives alongside a mentor, because guidance often matters as much as the funding itself.
slides.10: One clear solution really exists here today. Base aid on financial need, not only on test scores, so support actually reaches the students who require it the most.
slides.11: Money by itself is not the whole answer. Instead of handing out cash alone, schools could pair every scholarship with a genuine mentor who consistently guides the student.
slides.12: Waiting until university starts is already too late for many students. Support should begin much earlier, before kindergarten even, since the gap between rich and poor grows every single year.
slides.13: If aid and mentoring reach a student early enough, that student can finish a degree. That success can genuinely change their whole family's future, not just their own.
slides.14: However, a degree does not erase everything at once. It cannot pay off a family's old debt, and a richer graduate still starts with far more contacts and support.
slides.15: However, the entrance exam still rewards exactly what rich families can buy: years of paid lessons. So the same old cycle can quietly continue into the next generation.
slides.16: However, there is clearly one proven way forward here. Programs that combine funding with a mentor show the strongest results, and that mix actually breaks the old cycle.
slides.17: So what does the data actually show? Rich students still enter top schools more easily, yet the Stars Program and government aid are really helping poorer students catch up.
slides.18: This matters inside this very lecture room right now. Someone sitting near you may already hold exactly this particular scholarship themselves, so their story is not distant at all.
slides.19: So here is something you can actually do today. Volunteer to tutor a younger student, or push your school to attach a mentor to every scholarship it gives.
slides.20: Education should open the same door for every student, no matter how much money a family actually earns. Taiwan has only started that work, and it needs your generation to finish it.
